issues.legal_issue: A prior suit based on a claim to the entire property under a settlement deed does not bar a later partition suit based on a co-owner’s separate entitlement to a share when the causes of action differ.
material_facts: The earlier suit sought possession of the entire property on the basis of a settlement deed and was dismissed after the court did not accept the deed’s genuineness.
The later suit sought partition of a claimed half share based on the plaintiff’s asserted right as a co-owner.
The court found that the basis and cause of action of the two suits were different.
issues.conclusion: The earlier dismissal did not bar the later partition claim by res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 bars relitigation of an issue directly and substantially decided between the parties, but the bar requires that the subsequent claim be founded on the same cause of action and that the relief sought was available in the former proceeding. The court relied on Sulochanna Amma v. Narayanan Nair, Jaswant Singh v. Custodian of Evacuee Property, and Kunjan Nair Sivaraman Nair v. Narayanan Nair; cause of action comprises the facts necessary to support the claim to judgment.

predicates.partition_suit_after_prior_suit: A party brings a suit for partition after an earlier suit involving the same property and parties.
predicates.different_basis_of_claim: The later partition claim rests on a basis of entitlement distinct from the basis of the earlier claim for possession.

issues.definition: When a partition suit follows an earlier suit but rests on a different basis of entitlement, the earlier suit does not bar the partition claim.

issues.legal_issue: A co-owner’s exclusive possession does not by itself establish ouster or adverse possession against another co-owner.
material_facts: The plaintiff asserted that she had been dispossessed from the property in 1957.
The defendant claimed exclusive possession from 1956, payment of property taxes, and a patta in his name.
The defendant also pleaded hostile animus and exclusive possession, while the plaintiff sought partition as a co-owner.
issues.conclusion: Between co-owners, possession is presumed to be on behalf of all, and ouster requires more than sole possession and enjoyment; it requires an open hostile assertion, exclusive possession, and exercise of exclusive ownership to the other co-owner’s knowledge.
issues.legal_principle: A co-owner’s possession is presumed to be possession for all co-owners. Under P. Lakshmi Reddy v. R. Lakshmi Reddy, the possession must be adverse in continuity, publicity, and extent, and ouster requires an open assertion of hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment to the knowledge of the other co-owner. Vidya Devi v. Prem Prakash identifies hostile animus, long and uninterrupted possession, and open exercise of exclusive ownership to the other co-owner’s knowledge as necessary elements. The court also relied on Syed Shah Ghulam Ghouse Mohiuddin v. Syed Shah Ahmed Mohiuddin Kamisul Quadri.

predicates.co_owner_partition_case: A co-owner seeks partition of property held in common.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim: One co-owner claims that possession has become adverse to another co-owner.
predicates.exclusive_possession_alone: The asserted basis for adversity is exclusive possession without proof of open hostile assertion and exclusion to the other co-owner’s knowledge.

issues.definition: In a co-owner partition dispute, a claim based only on exclusive possession does not establish ouster.
